overview: Channel Infrastructure (formerly Refining NZ) owns and operates New Zealand's only fuel import terminal at Marsden Point, comprising deep-water jetties, ~290ML of active storage tanks, an Independent Petroleum Laboratory, and the country's only pipeline (170km) carrying liquid fuel to Auckland. Having closed its oil refinery in April 2022 and converted the site to an import-only terminal, the company now earns contracted, largely fixed and inflation-linked infrastructure income from three fuel majors (bp, Mobil, Z Energy) rather than volatile refining margins, and is pursuing a multi-decade redevelopment of its 180-hectare Marsden Point site (the 'Energy Precinct') alongside an international step-out into Melbourne's jet fuel supply chain (Somerton pipeline).

business_model.summary: Channel earns take-or-pay style infrastructure income under 10-year Terminal Services Agreements (from April 2022 to 2032) with bp, Mobil and Z Energy, covering 100% of its private storage and pipeline capacity. Revenue is a mix of fixed terminal fees, throughput/variable fees, and Contracted Storage Agreements (capacity-based fees for product storage and transmix handling, independent of throughput), plus a small fuel-testing laboratory business (IPL) and, from late 2025, a 25% interest in the Somerton jet fuel pipeline to Melbourne Airport. Nearly all Terminal Services and Contracted Storage fees escalate annually with NZ PPI (one-year lag), giving embedded inflation protection; new contracts since 2024 (Z Energy jet storage, NZ Government diesel storage, Higgins bitumen terminal, and an August 2026 15-year bp jet/diesel storage deal) are rapidly growing the contracted, largely fixed-fee revenue base. HY2026 revenue (continuing ops, excl. legacy Wiri lease) was $72.9m, +5% YoY, with EBITDA of $48.8m (67% margin); FY2026 EBITDA guidance has been raised three times in 2026 (from $95-100m to $97-105m to $103-108m as of August 2026), on a FY2025 base of $93.4m -- evidencing the business is now closer to a regulated-like infrastructure annuity than an industrial refiner.

revenue_streams.name: Terminal fees - fixed
revenue_streams.trend: stepping down per TSA schedule, offset by PPI

revenue_streams.name: Laboratory testing (IPL) and other (incl. Somerton pipeline)

business_model.customer_type: B2B, heavily concentrated -- three fuel majors (bp, Mobil, Z Energy) historically ~95% of revenue, plus the NZ Government (strategic diesel reserve, since mid-2026) and Higgins/Vinci (bitumen terminal tenant, from Q4 2026)
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand (~100% of legacy revenue, one reportable segment); international exposure since November 2025 via a 25% interest in the Somerton jet fuel pipeline serving Melbourne Airport, Australia (modest but growing contribution)

main_competitors: No direct domestic competitor for pipeline-delivered Auckland fuel supply
Alternative coastal import terminals/berths (smaller scale, no pipeline to Auckland)
Road/rail fuel logistics as a partial substitute for smaller volumes
Long-term substitute: EV/aviation decarbonisation reducing liquid fuel demand
competitive_position.market_position: Sole owner of New Zealand's only pipeline capable of transporting liquid fuel to Auckland; supplies ~40% of NZ's total liquid transport fuel demand and ~80% of NZ's jet fuel (including virtually all of Auckland International Airport's jet fuel). Effectively a natural monopoly infrastructure asset for the upper North Island, with growing optionality in Melbourne via Somerton.

moat_factors.description: Only deep-water harbour/jetty and only pipeline able to move liquid fuel to Auckland; replicating this would require immense capital, consenting and land access that competitors do not have

10-year Terminal Services Agreements with bp, Mobil and Z Energy (to 2032) covering 100% of private storage/pipeline capacity, now supplemented by a growing book of 10-19 year contracted storage deals (Z Energy jet, NZ Government diesel, Higgins bitumen, new bp jet/diesel storage), all with PPI-linked fee escalation

Exxon Mobil (~14%) and other fuel-major-related holders are also among Channel's largest shareholders, aligning incentives around long-term infrastructure economics rather than adversarial renegotiation

Designated critical national infrastructure; central to NZ's Minimum Stockholding Obligation and now hosts the country's first Government strategic diesel reserve (93 million litres), giving Channel quasi-regulatory standing and direct government relationships that are generating repeat, larger-scale contract wins

180 hectares of zoned industrial land (only ~1/3 utilised), with existing gas/water/electricity grid connections and 350+ million litres of brownfield storage capacity identified for repurposing, offering multiple option value pathways (biorefinery/SAF, hydrogen, diesel peaker, additional storage) without requiring greenfield permitting

weaknesses: Extreme customer concentration -- three counterparties (bp, Mobil, Z Energy) represent the substantial majority of contracted revenue; any credit or relationship deterioration is material

Structurally declining underlying volumes long-term as light vehicle EV penetration erodes petrol/diesel throughput (partially offset by fixed/take-or-pay fee structure); HY2026 petrol/diesel throughput was impacted by high fuel prices even though volumes tracked the Envisory outlook
Single-site concentration risk -- all core infrastructure sits at one coastal location exposed to storms, seismic and other physical/climate risks

Growth optionality (biorefinery, diesel peaker, Special Planning Zone) is largely third-party/consortium- and government-policy-dependent, with long lead times and uncertain final investment decisions -- the Marsden Point Biorefinery FID has now slipped again, from 2026 into 2027, due to a slower-than-expected consortium equity raise

Government/taxpayer deals (e.g., diesel reserve contract) attract political and media scrutiny over sole-source pricing, which is a reputational/regulatory risk even though currently revenue-accretive

Leverage is rising as growth capex accelerates -- net debt grew from $330m (FY2025) to $346m (HY2026) to $365m (Q3 2026 operational update), with leverage at 3.8x EBITDA at HY2026 (within the 3.0-4.5x target band but trending up)

growth_drivers: Marsden Point Energy Precinct redevelopment -- PwC estimates the projects under contemplation could add ~$3.3bn to NZ GDP and ~20,000 construction jobs, and ~$290m annual GDP plus ~1,150 FTE jobs once operational

New 15-year contract with bp (announced 27 August 2026) for additional jet and diesel fuel storage -- ~$130m of revenue over the initial term (before PPI indexation), funded by ~$65-70m of growth capex over 2026-2028 (tank repurposing starting September 2026, revenue from Q3 2028), the largest single contracted-storage win to date
Z Energy jet storage project completed in early July 2026, six months ahead of schedule and within budget, with ~$55m (pre-PPI) of revenue over 10 years now flowing from H2 2026
Higgins (Vinci Group) bitumen import terminal -- contract value increased to ~$57m over 15 years (from ~$45m), on track for completion late Q4 2026, expanding scope and capabilities

NZ Government strategic diesel reserve -- 93 million litres of dormant tank capacity recommissioned in only nine weeks (completed June 2026), generating ~$1.2m/month (~$14m full-year EBITDA contribution in 2027) under contract to end-2027; demonstrates Channel's ability to win larger, faster-turnaround government contracts, with the new bp deal partly a continuation of this fuel-security theme

Marsden Point Biorefinery consortium (Seadra Energy, with Qantas, Air New Zealand, Renova, Kent, ANZ Bank, Ballance Agri-Nutrients) targeting >$1bn private investment and up to 400 million litres/year of SAF, biodiesel, urea and fertiliser production; US$5.95m received for sale/removal of the decommissioned CCR Platformer unit (clearing the site); scope expanded in 2026 to include fertiliser manufacture via a Ballance Agri-Nutrients alliance; FID now expected to slip into 2027 given the consortium's slower equity raise

International step-out -- 25% acquisition of the Somerton jet fuel pipeline serving Melbourne Airport (A$14.1m, November 2025), cash-flow accretive from FY2026 (throughput broadly in line with expectations, though affected by Middle East-related schedule disruptions), with identified adjacent growth opportunities in the Melbourne jet fuel supply chain

Additional brownfield/greenfield optionality -- 350+ million litres of storage capacity identified for repurposing, 45 hectares available for new tank construction, an MoU with LanzaJet exploring an alcohol-to-jet facility, and a paused 72MW diesel-fired electricity peaking plant (FEED complete) pending Government LNG import facility decision
Dividend Reinvestment Plan (20.3% uptake at the September 2026 dividend) supporting balance sheet flexibility for growth funding

business.description: bp, Mobil and Z Energy account for the vast majority of contracted revenue; loss, distress, or aggressive renegotiation by any one materially impacts the business

EV penetration reduces petrol/diesel throughput over time; jet fuel grew 2.5% in HY2026 but Q2 2026 throughput was dented by elevated jet prices and reduced Middle Eastern carrier schedules; long-term aviation decarbonisation is a multi-decade risk, partly mitigated by fixed take-or-pay fee components and 'drop-in' biofuel compatibility

Biorefinery FID has slipped again into 2027 on a slower-than-expected consortium equity raise; the diesel peaker remains paused pending government LNG policy; other precinct projects depend on third-party consortium decisions and lengthy consenting, so final investment decisions can continue to slip

All critical assets (jetties, pipeline, tanks) concentrated at one coastal Northland site exposed to storms, seismic events and process safety incidents; two Lost Time Injuries recorded in HY2026 against a zero target

financial.description: Net debt rose from $330m (FY2025) to $346m (HY2026) to $365m (Q3 2026 update) as growth capex ramps (incl. the new bp contract's $65-70m spend and Somerton); leverage 3.8x EBITDA at HY2026 (up from 3.6x), within the broadened BBB/BBB+ shadow credit target of 3.0x-4.5x but with less headroom; CHI020 retail bond (maturing May 2027) refinancing options under review

Retained earnings remain deeply negative, offset by a large revaluation reserve from the FY2024 asset revaluation; equity quality is sensitive to future independent asset revaluations (reviewed at least every 3 years)
Somerton pipeline stake introduces AUD-denominated earnings and NZD/AUD translation risk as the Australian step-out grows

regulatory.description: Government mandates on fuel storage (28 days diesel by July 2028) are a growth driver today, but policy could shift (e.g., government choosing to own rather than rent storage, or alternative suppliers) reducing future government-linked revenue

Media/political criticism (e.g., NZ Herald) of the $21.6m diesel reserve deal as a non-competitive, politically-brokered arrangement creates reputational and potential future-tender risk, which could extend to scrutiny of subsequent large contracts

Provisions relate to legacy refinery shutdown, decommissioning and site restoration, including an ongoing legacy hydrocarbon plume requiring monitoring and remediation; HY2026 included a $7.2m non-cash credit from a jetty restoration provision reassessment, showing these estimates can move materially in either direction
December 2025 ASX foreign-exempt listing adds incremental compliance and one-off costs alongside NZX/FMA oversight

macro.risk: Global fuel/energy price and shipping shocks
macro.description: Fixed-fee-dominant model insulates Channel directly, but elevated fuel prices through HY2026 (linked partly to Middle East tensions) dampened petrol/diesel/jet throughput even as the same geopolitical backdrop drove government and bp fuel-security storage demand
Growing net debt ($365m at Q3 2026) with a weighted average 3.1-year debt maturity (HY2026); refinancing risk (CHI020 bond maturing May 2027) and higher-for-longer rates increase financing costs
Fixed take-or-pay revenue components provide resilience to NZ economic cycles, though variable/throughput fee components have some correlation to economic activity, fuel prices and transport demand

macro_factors.industry_outlook: New Zealand liquid fuel demand (petrol/diesel) is expected to plateau/gradually decline over the long term as EV penetration rises, per the Envisory forecast commissioned by Channel in 2024; HY2026 volumes tracked that outlook despite a high fuel price environment. Jet fuel demand continues to grow (HY2026 +2.5%), aided by Air New Zealand's widebody fleet returning to full service in June 2026 after engine shortage groundings, though exposed to Middle East-related schedule disruption. Government energy security policy (Minimum Stockholding Obligation, strategic reserves, and now a large new bp storage contract) is a structural tailwind for storage demand through at least 2028.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low to moderate -- majority of revenue is fixed/take-or-pay under long-term contracts with PPI escalation; variable/throughput fees provide modest cyclical sensitivity to fuel consumption, fuel prices and economic activity
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate and rising -- geared balance sheet (3.8x EBITDA net debt/EBITDA at HY2026, trending higher as growth capex ramps) with a 3.1-year weighted average debt maturity; higher rates increase financing costs and the CHI020 bond refinancing (due May 2027) is a near-term watch item
key_input_costs: Labour/salaries (up 12% YoY in HY2026 on inflation and new hires)
No longer exposed to crude oil/refining margin risk since 2022 conversion

recent_developments.event: Q3 2026 operational update: throughput 829 million litres (broadly flat YoY) despite high domestic fuel prices; 14 import shipments (vs 12 in Q3 2025); net borrowings rose to $365m; September dividend paid with 20.3% DRP uptake; bitumen terminal on track for late Q4 2026

Signed a new 15-year contract with bp for additional jet and diesel fuel storage at Marsden Point, worth ~$130m of revenue over the initial term (before indexation), funded by ~$65-70m of growth capex over 2026-2028 (tank repurposing from September 2026, revenue from Q3 2028) -- the largest contracted-storage win in Channel's history

HY2026 result (six months to 30 June 2026): revenue $72.9m (+4% reported, +5% underlying ex-Wiri), EBITDA $48.8m (67% margin), NPAT $19.3m (+47% YoY, partly aided by a $7.2m non-cash provision credit); interim dividend 7.25 cps (+16% YoY); FY2026 EBITDA guidance raised a third time in 2026, to $103-108m (from $97-105m in May, $95-100m in February)

NZ Government's first strategic diesel reserve (93 million litres, ~9 additional days of national diesel demand) brought into service at Marsden Point in only nine weeks; Z Energy jet storage project completed in early July 2026, six months ahead of the original schedule and within budget, with revenue now flowing from H2 2026

Agreed sale of the fully decommissioned CCR Platformer unit to Integrate Scope DMCC for US$5.95m, clearing the site for the Marsden Point Biorefinery and eliminating ~$3m of demolition provisions; biorefinery scope expanded to include fertiliser manufacture via a Ballance Agri-Nutrients alliance, but consortium equity raise delays mean FID is now expected to slip from 2026 into 2027

Raised FY2026 EBITDA guidance to $97-105m (from $95-100m), citing faster-than-expected government storage fill, the Z Energy jet tank running ~6 months ahead of schedule, and higher Higgins bitumen terminal contract value (revenue increased from ~$45m to ~$57m over the contract term)

Government committed up to $21.6m from the Regional Infrastructure Fund to Channel for additional diesel storage amid Middle East (Iran-related) fuel supply disruption concerns; deal drew media criticism (NZ Herald) over lack of competitive tender
FY2025 annual result: revenue $140.2m (+0.3% YoY), EBITDA $93.4m, Normalised FCF $66.9m (72% conversion), net debt $330m (3.6x EBITDA), FY2026 EBITDA guidance issued at $95-100m
Completed foreign exempt dual listing on the ASX (ticker CHI), broadening the institutional/retail shareholder base
Acquired 25% interest in the Somerton jet fuel pipeline to Melbourne Airport for A$14.1m (debt-funded) -- first international/Australian step-out, expected cash-flow accretive from FY2026

guidance.as_of: HY2026 result, 28 August 2026 (third upgrade of calendar 2026)

items.notes: Raised from $97-105m (May 2026), which itself was raised from the original $95-100m (Feb 2026); FY2025 actual was $93.4m. Driven by greater throughput visibility (8 months), on-plan delivery of the Government diesel storage contract, and the Z Energy jet tank completing 6 months ahead of schedule
Unchanged across all three FY2026 guidance updates; FY2025 actual was 8.8% of revenue; HY2026 actual was 11.7% of revenue, reflecting phasing of maintenance activity into H1
HY2026 conversion was 69% (vs 73% HY2025), reflecting increased payables and higher maintenance capex timing in H1

items.period: Ongoing (from May 2025 Capital Allocation Framework refresh)
items.notes: Interim FY2026 dividend of 7.25 cps, up 16% on HY2025's 6.25 cps
HY2026 leverage was 3.8x (up from 3.6x at FY2025) as growth capex (Somerton, Government diesel storage, bp contract) draws on debt facilities; gearing 31%, interest cover 5.7x, both within covenant

items.target: ~$9m (Z Energy jet storage + Higgins bitumen, full year) and ~$14m (NZ Government diesel storage, full year)
items.notes: Disclosed at HY2026 as incremental full-year contributions once these 2026-completed projects are running for a full 12 months in FY2027

Funds tank repurposing for the new 15-year bp jet/diesel storage contract (announced August 2026); funded from existing debt facilities; revenue (~$130m over the initial term, pre-indexation) begins Q3 2028; opex to rise $0.7-0.9m/year

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Rob Buchanan and CFO Alexa Preston characterised the third FY2026 guidance upgrade of the year as reflecting structural, contracted tailwinds -- 'greater certainty around fuel throughputs with eight months' visibility' and on-time, on-budget delivery of the Government diesel storage and Z Energy jet storage projects -- rather than one-off windfalls. Management reiterated the Marsden Point Energy Precinct as its number one growth priority, while flagging that the Biorefinery consortium's equity raise is 'taking longer than anticipated' and 'complex and ongoing,' with FID likely to extend into 2027; the Board continues to describe its posture on further M&A as a 'selective and disciplined approach to growth,' evaluating further step-out acquisitions in New Zealand and Australia alongside the three-pillar Energy Precinct strategy.

bull_case: Effectively a natural-monopoly infrastructure asset (sole pipeline to Auckland, deep-water jetties) generating highly predictable, PPI-linked, contracted cash flows through at least 2032 with investment-grade-quality fuel major counterparties, now reinforced by a landmark new 15-year, ~$130m bp storage contract (August 2026) on top of the Z Energy, NZ Government and Higgins deals signed since 2024

Demonstrated, repeated execution track record -- four consecutive years of on-time, on-budget project delivery, with the Z Energy jet tank and NZ Government diesel storage both completed early/ahead of schedule in 2026 -- underpinning management credibility for the much larger bp and biorefinery projects still to come

FY2026 EBITDA guidance has now been raised three times in a single year (from $95-100m in February to $103-108m by August), evidencing structural, not one-off, earnings momentum ahead of further contracted 2027 step-ups (~$9m from Z Energy/Higgins, ~$14m from Government diesel storage on a full-year basis)

Rising, well-covered dividend (interim FY2026 dividend 7.25 cps, +16% YoY) under a generous 70-90% Normalised FCF payout policy with a DRP option, appealing to income-focused NZX/ASX investors seeking a bond-like yield with contracted growth upside

Government/regulatory tailwinds (Minimum Stockholding Obligation tightening to 2028, strategic diesel reserve, geopolitically-driven fuel security demand) increasingly position Channel as a quasi-utility national-security asset capable of winning large new contracts from both government and its existing fuel-major customers
bear_case: Extreme customer concentration (three fuel majors plus a headline-risk-prone government contract) means the investment case rests on continued goodwill and contract renewal from a handful of counterparties; the stock has re-rated sharply (traded around 18x-20x EV/EBITDA versus a historical post-conversion average closer to 10x), leaving little room for disappointment, and consensus analyst price targets (~NZ$3.1-3.4) sit close to or below the recent share price

Leverage is climbing, not falling -- net debt rose from $330m (FY2025) to $365m (Q3 2026) and leverage from 3.6x to 3.8x EBITDA as growth capex (Somerton, Government diesel storage, and now $65-70m for the bp contract) draws on debt facilities, with the CHI020 retail bond refinancing (due May 2027) a near-term watch item

The most transformational growth option -- the Marsden Point biorefinery/SAF project -- has again slipped, with FID now expected to move from 2026 into 2027 due to a slower consortium equity raise, and other precinct projects (diesel peaker) remain on hold pending government LNG policy

Long-term structural volume decline from EV adoption in light vehicles, and eventual (if slower) aviation decarbonisation, works against throughput-linked revenue even though fixed fees provide a buffer; elevated fuel prices already dented petrol/diesel/jet volumes in HY2026

Political/media scrutiny of sole-sourced, non-competitive government contracts (diesel reserve) creates reputational and future-tender risk, and the growing scale of Channel's government and bp dealings raises the stakes if that scrutiny intensifies or if the government opts to build/own rather than rent strategic storage
